L4: # Help: PitchBook API
L5: 
L6: Find information about PitchBook’s API solution and discover how it can meet your business needs. Our API is a separate offering from the PitchBook Platform that requires a standalone contract agreement.
L7: ### Jump to
L8: 
L9:   * cite2†Overview L10:   * cite3†Use cases L11:   * cite4†How the API works L12: 
L13: Overview
L14: 
L15: PitchBook’s API solution allows you to call specific PitchBook data into your internal business systems on demand. This flexible solution means you have access to PitchBook’s expansive database. It’s the ideal integration for CRM enrichment, allowing you to extract data on an ad-hoc basis that meets the needs of your organization.
L16: You can explore a specific entity and retrieve valuable data, and the API solution enables you to apply specific criteria, such as location and industry, to drill down into the businesses you discover.
L17: ### Not a PitchBook customer?
L18: 
L19: cite5†Request free trial L20: 
L21: Use cases
L22: 
L23: The API is a good solution if:
L24: 
L25:   * Your scope and data points are subject to change frequently.
L26:   * You require a near-instant population of data.
L27:   * You perform ad-hoc research.
L28:   * You want to see past and present financial data.
L29:   * RESTful API is a system requirement.
L30: ### Ready to get started?
L31: 
L32: cite6†Log in†my.pitchbook.com L33: 
L34: How the API works
L35: 
L36: Accessing the API
L37: The PitchBook API is a RESTful implementation that most HTTP clients can easily access in your chosen language or via a web browser. Every call will use the same base URL: cite7†https://api.pitchbook.com†api.pitchbook.com L38: Available data points
L39: The API solution offers a variety of relational endpoints, including financing details, deal stock information, as well as AI-powered VC exit predictor data. See the full list from our cite8†API Endpoints Overview document.†pitchbook.highspot.com L40: 
L41: Create your API connection
L42: To start your API connection, you will need to send a request directly to our Direct Data team cite9†through this link. L43: Or if you’re a PitchBook client, you can also head to the Plugins & Apps section from the My PitchBook section of the left-hand sidebar on the PitchBook Platform and choose PitchBook API.
L44: 
L45: cite10†Image: Plugins and apps section of left-hand side-bar.jpg†pitchbook.brightspotcdn.com L46: 
L47: From this section on the platform, you can test specific endpoints. This section on PitchBook also allows you to reach out to our Direct Data team to request access to the API.
L48: ##
L49: ## Next steps
L50: 
L51: Our team will work with you to understand the insights and data you’re looking for and help you establish the API connection through an API key or authentication token. Available data for each entity type is packaged across several endpoints so you can map the data to your desired format and structure.

L464: Senior Technical Content Writer
L465: For years, authenticating to cite143†Datadog APIs†docs.datadoghq.com meant managing two separate credentials: an API key and an application key. That model worked well when most API activity came from developers running scripts or a small number of integrations. But modern infrastructure looks very different. Today, Datadog APIs are accessed by cite144†CI/CD pipelines , Terraform workflows, autonomous systems, and increasingly, AI agents operating across teams and environments.
L466: To support those new access patterns, Datadog is introducing a new authentication model built around four purpose-specific approaches: cite145†Personal Access Tokens (PATs)†docs.datadoghq.com , cite146†Service Access Tokens (SATs)†docs.datadoghq.com , workload identity federation, and customer-managed OAuth clients. Together, these capabilities provide scoped, identity-aware authentication designed for both human users and non-human workloads.
L467: 
L468: In this post, we’ll discuss:
L469:   * cite147†Why Datadog is updating its API authentication L470: 
L471:   * cite148†Datadog’s new API authentication model L472: 
L473:   * cite149†What happens to existing application keys L474: 
L475:   * cite150†How to choose the right authentication model for your use case L476: ## cite147†Why Datadog is updating its API authentication L477: 
L478: The original Datadog authentication model separated telemetry ingestion from API authorization. API keys identified the Datadog organization receiving data, while application keys identified the user performing an action. This dual-key model worked well when user identities mapped to individual developers. However, this model did not map cleanly to automated workflows such as CI/CD pipelines, which do not have a single human owner.
L479: AI agents acting on behalf of human users introduced another challenge for the existing model. When cite151†the Datadog MCP Server†docs.datadoghq.com calls an API to retrieve a monitor’s status, how do we determine who authorized the request, what scope was granted, and how long that access should last? Security and compliance teams also need to know exactly who accessed what data, and when that access occurred. Application key usage alone does not provide enough context for detailed audit attribution.
L480: To address these challenges, Datadog is introducing authentication models designed around specific access patterns. Instead of relying on a single credential type for every workflow, teams can now use credentials tailored to developers, automation systems, cloud-native workloads, and delegated application access. In the following sections, we’ll look at how each authentication model works and where it fits best.
L481: ## cite148†Introducing Datadog’s new API authentication model L482: 
L483: Our updated authentication model replaces the application key with four targeted alternatives, each designed for a specific access pattern.
L484: ### cite152†Personal Access Tokens: for developer workflows L485: 
L486: PATs are designed for developers who directly interact with Datadog APIs. They are intended for user-driven workflows such as building CLI tools, writing scripts against the API, or pulling data from Datadog into custom applications and dashboards.
L487: PATs are scoped to the permissions of the user who creates them and require an expiration window to avoid reliance on long-lived credentials. Because PATs are tied directly to a user identity, cite153†Audit Trail†docs.datadoghq.com logs can attribute API activity to a specific user. When a user loses access to an organization, their PATs are revoked alongside their account access.
L488: ### cite154†Service Access Tokens: for automation and autonomous AI agents L489: 
L490: SATs are designed for automation systems and non-human workloads that need persistent access to Datadog APIs. Common examples include CI/CD pipelines, Terraform runs, infrastructure automation, and autonomous AI agents operating without a human in the loop.
L491: SATs are tied to a service account, not an individual user. The service account has its own permissions, independent of any individual on your team. Like PATs, SATs are scoped and support configurable expiration policies. Unlike old application keys, SATs include readable prefixes (`ddsat_`) and identifiable public portions, making credentials easier to track and manage.
L492: ### cite155†Workload identity federation: for cloud-native workloads L493: If your workload runs on AWS, cite156†it already has an IAM identity†docs.aws.amazon.com . Workload identity federation, a system that establishes trust between two parties for user authentication and resource access, enables AWS workloads to authenticate directly to Datadog by binding an AWS IAM role to a Datadog service account. Instead of creating and storing static Datadog credentials, the workload uses its existing cloud identity to access Datadog APIs.
L494: This removes the need to store API credentials in secrets managers, CI/CD pipelines, or configuration files for workloads such as Terraform runners and the Datadog Agent. Teams can manage access through existing IAM policies rather than rotating and distributing long-lived credentials.
L495: 
L496: Workload identity federation is generally available for AWS workloads, with support for additional cloud providers planned for the future.
L497: ### cite157†OAuth clients: for delegated and temporary AI agent access L498: 
L499: OAuth clients are designed for AI agents that need temporary, scoped access to Datadog APIs. OAuth supports both delegated access, where an application acts on behalf of a user, and machine-to-machine (M2M) access for autonomous systems operating without a human in the loop.
L500: In delegated workflows, users explicitly approve the scopes an application or AI agent can access before the application receives a short-lived token. This gives organizations more granular control over who authorized the request, what permissions were granted, and how long that access should last.

L54: cite2†Sign up cite2†Open app L55: # Getting started
L56: 
L57: Linear’s public API is built using GraphQL. It’s the same API we use internally for developing our applications. If you are new to GraphQL, Apollo has cite35†resources for beginners†blog.apollographql.com . The official cite36†GraphQL documentation†graphql.org is another good starting point.
L58: 
L59: ## Endpointcite37†⁠ L60: 
L61: Linear’s GraphQL endpoint is:
L62: 
L63:     `https://api.linear.app/graphql`
L64: 
L65: It supports introspection so you can query the whole schema.
L66: ## Authenticationcite38†⁠ L67: 
L68: The Linear API supports personal API keys and OAuth2 authentication.
L69: ### OAuthcite39†⁠ L70: 
L71: If you’re building an application for others to use, we recommend you use cite12†OAuth2 authentication . Once you complete the authentication flow and acquire an access token, pass it with the header `Authorization: Bearer <ACCESS_TOKEN>`
L72: 
L73:     `curl \
L74:       -X POST \
L75:       -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
L76:       -H "Authorization: Bearer <ACCESS_TOKEN>" \
L77:       --data '{ "query": "{ issues { nodes { id title } } }" }' \
L78:       https://api.linear.app/graphql`
L79: ### Personal API Keyscite40†⁠ L80: 
L81: For personal scripts API keys are the easiest way to access the API. Visit cite41†Security & access settings to create and manage them.
L82: 
L83: To authenticate your requests, you need to pass the API key with header: `Authorization: <API_KEY>`
L84: 
L85:     `curl \
L86:       -X POST \
L87:       -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
L88:       -H "Authorization: <Replace this with your API Key>" \
L89:       --data '{ "query": "{ issues { nodes { id title } } }" }' \
L90:       https://api.linear.app/graphql`
L91: ## Error handlingcite42†⁠ L92: 
L93: Linear’s GraphQL API follows the standard GraphQL error format, returning errors within an errors array in the response. Each error object includes a message describing what went wrong, a path array indicating where in the query the
L94: error occurred, and extensions that may contain additional context such as error codes or validation details.
L95: Always check for the errors array before assuming success—GraphQL queries can partially succeed with a 200 HTTP status, returning some data while
L96: including errors for failed fields. Monitor HTTP status codes for server errors (5xx) and make sure to correctly handle cite6†rate limits . Use strongly-typed GraphQL clients when possible to catch validation errors at development time, and always validate required fields to avoid runtime null value errors.
L97: ## Linear SDKcite43†⁠ L98: 
L99: The cite21†Linear SDK exposes the Linear GraphQL schema, and makes it easy to access models, or perform mutations. We recommend using it to interact with the GraphQL API. It is written in TypeScript, allowing all operations to be strongly typed.
L100: ## Getting Startedcite44†⁠ L101: 
L102: We recommend using a GraphQL client to introspect and explore the schema if you are not using the Linear Client (SDK).
L103: 
L104: Our GraphQL API is explorable and queryable via cite45†Apollo Studio†studio.apollographql.com , no download or log in required. Click the Schema tab to browse the schema, and click the Explorer tab to run queries.
L105: 
L106: Once you have your client installed, you can start making queries (read) and mutations (write) to the API.
L107: ### Queries & Mutationscite46†⁠ L108: 
L109: To get information about the authenticated user, you can use the `viewer` query:
L110: 
L111:     `query Me {
L112:       viewer {
L113:         id
L114:         name
L115:         email
L116:       }
L117:     }`
L118: 
L119: As issues (and most other objects) are team based, you first need to get the ID of the team you want to interact with:
L120: 
L121:     `query Teams {
L122:       teams {
L123:         nodes {
L124:           id
L125:           name
L126:         }
L127:       }
L128:     }`
L129: Once you have found the correct team, you can get the issues for that team. Lets make a request with also some other issue metadata:
L130: 
L131:     `query Team {
L132:       team(id: "9cfb482a-81e3-4154-b5b9-2c805e70a02d") {
L133:         id
L134:         name
L135: 
L136:         issues {
L137:           nodes {
L138:             id
L139:             title
L140:             description
L141:             assignee {
L142:               id
L143:               name
L144:             }
L145:             createdAt
L146:             archivedAt
L147:           }
L148:         }
L149:       }
L150:     }`
L151: We can also get an issue by id:
L152: 
L153:     `query Issue {
L154:       issue(id: "BLA-123") {
L155:         id
L156:         title
L157:         description
L158:       }
L159:     }`
L160: 
L161: Locate the IDs of teams, issues and other entities directly within Linear itself from the command menu: `Cmd/Ctrl+K` and “Copy model UUID”. This will show results based on the page you’re currently viewing within Linear.
L162: ### Creating & Editing Issuescite47†⁠ L163: 
L164: To create a new issue, use a mutation:
L165: 
L166:     `mutation IssueCreate {
L167:       issueCreate(
L168:         input: {
L169:           title: "New exception"
L170:           description: "More detailed error report in markdown"
L171:           teamId: "9cfb482a-81e3-4154-b5b9-2c805e70a02d"
L172:         }
L173:       ) {
L174:         success
L175:         issue {
L176:           id
L177:           title
L178:         }
L179:       }
L180:     }`
L181: This mutation will create a new issue and return its `id` and `title` if the call was successful (`success: true`).
L182: 
L183: If an issue is created without a specified `stateId`(the status field for the issue), the issue will be assigned to the team’s first state in the Backlog workflow state category. If the “Triage” feature is turned on for the team, then the issue will be assigned to the Triage workflow state.
